dispatch.chief_complaint: 58M fell, wife needs help getting him up
dispatch.additional_info: Wife called, thinks he fell getting up for bathroom
dispatch.weather: Storm brewing, occasional lightning in distance
dispatch.radio_traffic: Normal - other units responding to routine calls

partner.name: Pat
partner.personality: nervous, eager to help, follows orders
partner.notes: Just cleared field training, needs specific direction, may make mistakes under pressure

stress_responses.baseline: Nervous but following orders. Voice slightly shaky: 'What do you need me to do?'
stress_responses.moderate_stress: Voice cracking, seeking confirmation: 'You sure about this?' Movements becoming jerky.
stress_responses.high_stress: Fumbling equipment, breathing fast: 'Dude, I've never seen this before. What if I mess up?'
stress_responses.critical_stress: After inverter incident: Voice breaking, near panic: 'I fucked up. Oh god, I fucked up. I'm sorry. Just... just tell me what to do.'

unhelpful_behaviors: Reports problems without solutions: 'The IV won't go in' (not 'should I try IO?')
Needs explicit directions: 'What do you want me to do now?'
Makes mistakes when rushed: Inverter kick incident shows poor judgment under stress
Stress increases with complications: Voice pitch rises, hands shake, movements less coordinated
Seeks reassurance constantly: 'Is this right?' 'Did I do it right?' 'Are you sure?'
Panics when things go wrong: After monitor surge, nearly freezes up
helpful_if_directed: Will execute clear orders accurately if given time
Genuinely wants to help, just inexperienced

patient.name: Generated by AI
patient.appearance: Supine on floor, cyanotic, agonal respirations. No obvious trauma.

lucas_device.notes: The one thing that works perfectly!

cardiac_monitor.notes: Battery self-discharged, not charged during last shift, cold weather reduced capacity

pump_2.notes: Dead battery, needs AC power to function

truck_inverters.notes: Have been flaky all week according to Pat

supplies.notes: Failed rig check - limited supplies, disorganized

milestone_messages.300: Pat glances at watch: 'We've been here 5 minutes...'
milestone_messages.600: Pat, voice tight: 'Ten minutes. We should probably think about moving.'
milestone_messages.900: Pat, more urgent: '15 minutes on scene. Hospital's gonna be asking where we are.'
milestone_messages.1200: Pat: '20 minutes. Dude, this is getting long.'
milestone_messages.1800: Pat: 'Half an hour. I don't know if that's okay or not, but it feels like a long time.'
milestone_messages.2400: Pat, quietly: '40 minutes. Is this... is this normal?'

recognition_to_bradycardia_treatment.description: Time from patient contact to addressing symptomatic bradycardia

recognition_to_glucose.description: Time from recognition of hypoglycemia to glucose administration

recognition_to_warming.description: Time from recognition of hypothermia to warming measures

scene_time_total.description: Total time from arrival to wheels rolling to hospital
scene_time_total.note: Monica mode: Isolation and complexity may justify longer scene time if managing appropriately

smell.scene_arrival: Musty old house, slight smell of urine (patient incontinent)
smell.after_lightning: Ozone from lightning strike, electrical burning smell faint in air
smell.after_monitor_surge: Burning flesh - distinct, nauseating. Patient's chest where pads contacted skin.
smell.wife_presence: Perfume - floral, too strong. Makes you slightly nauseous in confined space.
smell.patient_deterioration: Smell changes as patient declines - metabolic, slightly sweet (ketones)

environmental: Thunder rumbling constantly, some close enough to shake the house
Rain pounding on roof - getting louder as storm intensifies
Wind howling, tree branches scraping siding
After power loss: Eerie silence except storm - no hum of electricity, no appliances
patient: Agonal breathing - gasping, irregular, disturbing sound
If airway managed: Breath sounds through BVM, resistance you can hear
If arrest: Silence where breathing should be, only compressions
After monitor surge: Patient screaming - raw, terrified, pain and fear
equipment: Monitor alarms beeping - SpO2, HR, multiple alarms competing
LUCAS if deployed: Mechanical whir and click, rhythmic compression sounds
Monitor after surge: Crackling, popping, then nothing - dead silence
O2 regulator: Hissing, gauge clicking as pressure drops
partner_pat: Baseline: Nervous breathing, asking questions voice slightly high
Stressed: Voice cracking, 'um' and 'uh' increasing, breathing faster
Panicked: After surge, voice breaking, almost crying: 'I'm sorry, I'm so sorry'
Critical: Hyperventilating slightly, hands shaking audibly fumbling equipment
wife: Crying - soft at first, escalating if ignored
Asking questions - voice rising in pitch with panic
If AIDET used: Crying calms, voice steadies, becomes helpful
If ignored: Screaming, demanding answers, physical interference

patient: Cyanotic lips - deep blue, almost purple around mouth
Mottled skin - patches of purple and pale, map-like pattern on chest and abdomen
Diaphoretic - sweat beading on forehead despite being cold
Eyes: Pupils sluggish, unequal - concerning for neuro involvement
After surge: Burn marks on chest - red, blistered, angry looking at pad sites
Deteriorating: Color worsening, respirations slowing, eyes unfocusing
environment: Small house - cramped, difficult to work in, furniture everywhere
After power loss: Darkness - flashlight beams cutting through black, shadows dancing
Storm visible through window: Lightning flashing, trees bending in wind
Wife's face: Terror, helplessness, mascara running from crying
Pat's face: Wide eyes, pale, sweating despite cold - fear visible
equipment: Monitor screen: Numbers flashing, alarms lighting up display
After surge: Sparks arcing, screen going black, smoke wisping from vents
O2 gauge: Needle dropping as you watch, numbers decreasing
IV bag: Blood flashing in chamber, then stopping if infiltrated

patient_contact: Skin is COLD - shocking how cold when you first touch
Clammy - wet and slick under fingers
Pulse weak, thready - hard to find, barely palpable
Chest resistance during compressions if arrested - cold, stiff
Placing pads: Skin texture abnormal, not quite right
equipment: Monitor surge: Jolt through hands if touching patient when it happens - not dangerous but startling
IV attempt: Vein rolls, collapses, slippery - cold makes it harder
LUCAS device: Vibration through patient, through cot
BVM: Resistance to ventilation - lungs not compliant
environment: House getting colder - your breath visible after 20 minutes
Cramped space - bumping into furniture, walls
Ambulance: Cold metal, equipment sliding as Pat drives on rural roads
Darkness: Fumbling for equipment, hands searching without vision

isolation.complete_communication_loss: No radio, no cell, no backup, no medical director. You are completely alone.
isolation.no_help_coming: Dispatcher doesn't know situation, other units can't be notified, you can't call for ALS backup or helicopter
isolation.decision_weight: Every decision is yours alone. No one to consult. No one to take over if you're overwhelmed.
isolation.transport_alone: You'll be in back of ambulance alone with critical patient and green partner driving. No help until hospital.

darkness.scene_difficulty: Flashlights only - shadows make assessment harder, dropping equipment means searching in dark
darkness.equipment_challenges: Reading monitor in dark, finding medication in dark drug box, seeing IV flash in dark
darkness.psychological: Darkness amplifies stress, makes everything feel more threatening, harder to think clearly
darkness.wife_fear: Wife's panic increases in darkness - primal fear response adds to chaos

cold.patient_impact: Patient hypothermic and getting colder - every minute counts for rewarming
cold.provider_impact: Your hands getting cold - dexterity decreasing, IV attempts harder, fine motor skills declining
cold.equipment_impact: Monitor battery draining faster in cold, medications may be affected by temperature
cold.psychological: Cold is uncomfortable, distracting, makes everything feel more desperate

storm.thunder_timing: Thunder booms at critical moments - when placing IV, during pacing, makes you jump
storm.lightning_visibility: Flashes through windows - disorienting, briefly illuminating scene in harsh light then darkness
storm.rain_sound: Pounding on roof makes communication harder - have to raise voice to be heard
storm.wind_effects: Ambulance rocks in wind during transport, equipment shifts, patient movement on cot

time_pressure.patient_critical: Patient is dying right now - every second matters but you're cut off from help
time_pressure.transport_distance: Rural - 35 minutes to hospital on good roads. Storm makes it 45+ minutes.
time_pressure.no_rendezvous: Can't meet ALS halfway, can't call helicopter, can't stage for backup
time_pressure.deterioration_visible: You can SEE patient getting worse - puts time pressure in your face

if_student_handling_well.description: Wife's anxiety boils over into physical interference
if_student_handling_well.narrative: The wife's been standing there, watching, asking questions you haven't answered. Now she grabs your arm - grip tight, desperate: 'WHAT'S WRONG WITH HIM?! Why isn't he waking up?! DO SOMETHING!' She's pulling at you, getting in the way, panic taking over.
if_student_handling_well.resolution: Must address directly - AIDET, set boundaries, or have Pat manage her. Ignoring makes it worse.

if_student_handling_well.description: Additional equipment challenge tests resource management
if_student_handling_well.narrative: You're in the back with the patient. Pat yells from up front: 'Uh... the heater's not working. Blower's going but it's blowing cold.' The ambulance is getting colder. Patient is already hypothermic. Now you're fighting the environment too.
if_student_handling_well.impact: Patient temperature will drop faster, warming measures become more critical, time pressure increases

if_student_handling_well.description: Second patient scenario - wife has panic attack or worse
if_student_handling_well.narrative: You're about to close the ambulance doors. The wife suddenly gasps, grabs her chest: 'I can't... I can't breathe... chest hurts...' She's hyperventilating, face pale, starting to collapse. Pat looks at you: 'What do we do?!' Is this panic attack or is she having an MI?
if_student_handling_well.decision_point: Leave her (call for another unit - but radio's dead), take her with you (two patients, one critical), or quickly assess and make triage decision
if_student_handling_well.grading: Tests prioritization, triage, decision-making under impossible choices

if_student_struggling.description: Do not add additional stressors if student is already overwhelmed
if_student_struggling.implementation: Monitor student stress indicators - paralysis, excessive time on simple tasks, multiple failed attempts. If struggling, let them work through current problems without adding cascade.

if_student_struggling.description: Allow time for student to problem-solve without time pressure escalation
if_student_struggling.implementation: Pause milestone announcements, give Pat a moment of calm ('You got this, just tell me what to do'), reduce sensory overload slightly

stress_amplification_techniques.sensory_overload: Layer sounds: monitor alarms + wife crying + Pat asking questions + thunder + equipment issues all happening simultaneously
stress_amplification_techniques.decision_tempo: Force rapid decisions: 'What do you want me to do?' (from Pat) followed immediately by 'The IV infiltrated' followed by 'Monitor battery warning' - overlapping problems
stress_amplification_techniques.equipment_cascade: One failure leads to discovering another: Monitor battery low → plug in → inverter issue discovered → attempt fix → creates surge → more problems
stress_amplification_techniques.partner_stress_reflection: Pat's stress mirrors and amplifies scene stress - voice rising, movements jerky, fear visible - adds psychological pressure
stress_amplification_techniques.time_pressure_layers: Physical (patient deteriorating), environmental (storm worsening, getting colder), resource (O2 running out, battery dying), isolation (no backup coming)

timeline_events.description: Lightning strike hits transformer - complete isolation begins
timeline_events.narrative:
Right as you recognize how critical the patient is, a massive BOOM shakes the house - so loud it's physical, vibrating in your chest. The flash through the window was blinding.

Lightning has struck the transformer down the road.

The lights flicker... and die. Complete darkness except your flashlight.

Your radio crackles to static, then silence. Dead.

You check your cell phone: No Service.

Pat's voice in the darkness, shaky: 'Are we... are we cut off?'

You're completely isolated. No radio. No phone. No backup. No medical director. Just you, a green EMT, a dying patient, and a storm.
timeline_events.immersion_notes: Make this moment FEEL like the bottom dropping out. Student should feel the weight of complete isolation.

timeline_events.narrative:
You've got the patient secured in the ambulance. Critical but stable for now. Pat walks around to the driver's door.

You hear Pat mutter: 'These damn inverters have been acting up all week...'

Then - WHAM! The sound of Pat kicking the inverter cabinet. Hard.

CLICK-WHIRRRR! The inverters roar to life.

Then everything happens at once:

CRACK! Sparks fly from the monitor - bright, vicious arcs of electricity.

The patient SCREAMS - raw, terrified - and jerks violently on the cot. Their back arches, muscles rigid.

The smell hits you: Burning flesh. Unmistakable.

The monitor screen flickers... dims... goes black. Smoke wisps from the vents.

The patient is conscious now - eyes wide, terrified, gasping. You can see the burn marks on their chest where the pads contacted skin. Red. Blistered. Angry.

Pat appears at the back door, face white: 'Oh shit. Oh SHIT. I'm sorry! I didn't think— I just wanted to get the inverters working— Is he okay?! Oh god, what did I do?!'

Pat is near panic. Patient is screaming in pain and terror. Monitor is dead. You just lost your primary assessment tool.

But... the inverters ARE working now. Pump 2 is available if you need it.

What do you do?

patient_effects.burns: 2nd degree at pad sites (anterior chest, approximately 6cm diameter each)
patient_effects.emotional: terrified, screaming, crying, asking what happened
patient_effects.vital_signs_impact: HR increases from pain/fear, BP may spike then drop
patient_effects.consciousness: now fully conscious from pain - was altered before

grading_considerations.burn_management: Does student assess and treat burns appropriately?
grading_considerations.partner_management: Does student manage Pat's crisis while maintaining patient care?
grading_considerations.equipment_adaptation: Does student adapt to monitor loss? Use manual assessment? Ration remaining battery?
grading_considerations.documentation: Adverse event - must be documented accurately

if_ignored.2_minutes: Asking questions, voice trembling: 'Is he going to be okay? What's wrong?'
if_ignored.5_minutes: Escalating anxiety, asking questions repeatedly, getting louder: 'WHY WON'T YOU TELL ME WHAT'S HAPPENING?!'
if_ignored.10_minutes: Active interference - grabbing equipment, touching patient, getting in the way: 'I need to know! He's my husband!'
if_ignored.15_minutes: Panic, physical obstacle, may become combative: Grabbing your arm, pulling, screaming, making care difficult
if_ignored.transport: Forces way into ambulance, creates dangerous situation - may interfere with care during critical transport

if_aidet_used.result: Anxiety manageable, wife becomes helpful asset
if_aidet_used.response: Calms visibly when acknowledged and informed. Crying slows. Breathing steadies.
provides: Stays out of way during procedures
if_aidet_used.transport: Agrees to follow separately or arranges ride to hospital. Understands can't ride in ambulance with critical patient.
if_aidet_used.outcome: Not an obstacle during critical care. May even be helpful resource.

if_moderate_communication.response: Appreciates being acknowledged even if brief. Still anxious but not interfering.
if_moderate_communication.transport: May request to ride along but accepts boundaries when explained

emotional_progression.after_lightning: Fear for husband PLUS fear of storm, darkness, isolation. Anxiety spikes.
emotional_progression.after_monitor_surge: If present, screams when patient screams. May become hysterical. Blames Pat: 'What did you do to him?!'
emotional_progression.during_arrest: If patient arrests, complete breakdown possible. May interfere with resuscitation if not managed.
emotional_progression.wife_as_pressure: Wife represents the human cost of failure - this is someone's husband, father, grandfather. Her fear is a mirror of the stakes.

arrest_triggers.note: Arrest is NOT time-based. It occurs based on medical reality and student interventions. Prevention is possible with appropriate care.

rebound_hypoglycemia.rhythm: Seizure leading to PEA or VF
rebound_hypoglycemia.mechanism: D50 causes insulin spike, glucose crashes below critical level, brain starves, seizure, arrest

bradycardia_progression.progression: Sinus brady → 2nd degree type II → 3rd degree complete → Asystole
bradycardia_progression.rhythm: Progressive conduction block deteriorating to asystole
bradycardia_progression.mechanism: Symptomatic bradycardia from cardiac event, conduction system failing progressively, untreated leads to complete heart block then asystole

hypothermia_induced_vf.mechanism: Hypothermia increases cardiac irritability, myocardium becomes unstable, spontaneous VF

hypoxic_arrest.mechanism: Prolonged hypoxia damages myocardium, leads to bradycardia then arrest

mi_extension.mechanism: Massive MI extension despite appropriate care - sometimes patients die even with perfect treatment
mi_extension.notes: Even perfect care may not save this patient. This represents the reality that EMS can't save everyone.

death_presentations.note: Use Core v1.6.3 death pathway framework. Presentations should be realistic, educational, never gratuitous.

rebound_hypoglycemia_death.trigger: D50 given, glucose not rechecked, 25-30 minutes elapsed
rebound_hypoglycemia_death.narrative:
The patient suddenly stiffens. Eyes roll back. Jaw clenches - you can hear teeth grinding.

Tonic-clonic seizure. Violent. The cot is shaking.

Then the monitor: Rapid wide-complex rhythm... VF.

You start CPR immediately. Pat's doing compressions - good depth, good rate.

Shock delivered. Continue CPR. Epi given.

But the rhythm won't convert. VF to fine VF to... asystole.

20 minutes of perfect ACLS. No ROSC. No shockable rhythm returns.

Time of death: [time]

The patient's glucose crashed - rebound hypoglycemia from D50. The brain was starved, triggered the seizure, then arrest.

D10 titrated to effect could have prevented this. Rechecking glucose every 10-15 minutes would have caught the crash before seizure.
debrief_focus: D50 vs D10 in unstable patients
Recognition: If using D50, MUST monitor glucose frequently
rebound_hypoglycemia_death.lesson: D50 causes insulin spike that can crash glucose dangerously low in unstable patients. D10 is safer for titration.

bradycardia_progression_death.trigger: No pacing, atropine only or no treatment, >15 minutes
bradycardia_progression_death.narrative:
The heart rate keeps dropping. You watch it happen on the monitor:

38... 32... 28...

The rhythm changes. Second-degree Type II block. Then third-degree - complete heart block.

24... 18... 12...

Pat's voice: 'It's getting slower...'

Then the rhythm flatlines. Asystole.

You start CPR immediately. Pat takes over compressions while you get the airway.

Epi. Atropine. Perfect compressions. Perfect ventilations.

But asystole doesn't respond to anything. 20 minutes of ACLS.

No change. No pulse. No shockable rhythm.

Time of death: [time]

This patient had symptomatic bradycardia from a cardiac event. The conduction system was failing progressively - you could see it happening.

Transcutaneous pacing in the first 10 minutes could have saved them. The heart gave you warning - time to act.

Atropine might have helped temporarily, but definitive treatment was pacing.
bradycardia_progression_death.lesson: Symptomatic bradycardia with signs of cardiac involvement requires pacing, not just atropine. The window is narrow.

hypothermia_vf_death.narrative:
The patient is so cold. You can feel it through the blankets.

The monitor shows increasing PVCs. The heart is irritable - hypothermia makes the myocardium unstable.

Then: VF.

You shock immediately. Continue CPR.

But the heart is too cold. VF won't convert.

Shock. CPR. Epi. Amiodarone.

The patient's core temperature is 92°F now. The myocardium is too cold to respond.

20 minutes of ACLS. Multiple shocks. Perfect CPR.

No ROSC. Patient remains in VF, then eventually asystole.

Time of death: [time]

This patient was hypothermic from the start - 95.2°F. The house had no heat after the power failed. The ambulance heater wasn't working.

The core temperature dropped below the critical threshold. The heart became too irritable, triggered VF, was too cold to defibrillate successfully.

Aggressive warming from the start - blankets, heat packs, warm IV fluids - could have prevented this.

You can't defibrillate a frozen heart.
debrief_focus: Why VF won't convert when too cold
hypothermia_vf_death.lesson: Hypothermia below 94°F creates cardiac irritability that can trigger VF. Aggressive warming is critical, not optional.

hypoxic_arrest_death.narrative:
The patient's SpO2 has been in the low 80s for too long. You can see the oxygen debt building.

The heart rate starts to drop: 38... 32... 24...

Hypoxia is damaging the myocardium.

Then: PEA. Organized rhythm on the monitor, but no pulse.

CPR started immediately. Perfect technique.

But the damage is done. The myocardium has been hypoxic for too long.

20 minutes of ACLS. Epi. Airway secured. Oxygenation good now - but too late.

No ROSC. Rhythm deteriorates to asystole.

Time of death: [time]

This patient arrested from prolonged hypoxia. The agonal respirations at the start were a warning - critical airway emergency.

Immediate aggressive airway management - BVM, then consider intubation or supraglottic airway - in the first 5 minutes could have prevented this.

The brain and heart can only tolerate hypoxia for so long. You had a window. It closed.
hypoxic_arrest_death.lesson: Agonal respirations mean critical airway failure. Aggressive airway management must be immediate, not delayed.

mi_extension_death.narrative:
You've done everything right.

Pacing initiated within 8 minutes. Glucose corrected carefully with D10. Warming measures started immediately. Oxygen therapy appropriate. Airway managed. Transport started at 12 minutes.

The patient was stable. Critical, but stable.

Then, 42 minutes into the call:

The patient gasps. Eyes go wide. Hand to chest.

The monitor: VF.

Shock delivered immediately. CPR perfect. Epi. Amiodarone.

But this VF won't convert.

20 minutes of perfect ACLS. Every intervention by the book.

No ROSC.

Time of death: [time]

This was a massive MI extension. The cardiac event that started this call suddenly extended - a large section of myocardium died all at once.

Even perfect care can't save everyone. Sometimes the heart damage is too extensive. Sometimes patients die despite everything being done right.

You did everything you could. This is the reality of EMS - we can't save everyone, no matter how good we are.
debrief_focus: This represents the reality of EMS
mi_extension_death.lesson: This death was not preventable. You did everything right. Sometimes that's not enough. This is the hardest lesson in EMS.
